meta.title: Two Graphing Stories — Modeling Physical Motion
meta.pageTitle: Two Graphing Stories: Motion & Coordinate Modeling | Hesten's Learning
meta.description: Can a picture tell two different stories? Translate physical events into piecewise mathematical graphs and discover how slope reveals velocity, rest intervals, and elevation changes.
meta.pageDescription: Connect physical motion stories to piecewise coordinate graphs of elevation and speed with animated real-time simulators.
meta.author: Hesten's Learning Team

overview.title: Student & Teacher Overview: Lesson 5
overview.text: In this lesson, you will analyze two classic motion scenarios: a hiker descending and ascending a canyon (Elevation vs. Time) and a skateboarder accelerating down a ramp and coasting across flat ground (Speed vs. Time). Use the animated simulator below to link physical motion directly with piecewise coordinate graphs.
outcomes: Match physical motion scenarios with piecewise continuous functions and coordinate graphs.
Distinguish between an Elevation vs. Time graph (where $y$ represents physical vertical altitude) and a Speed vs. Time graph (where $y$ represents rate of motion).
Interpret the physical meaning of negative, positive, and zero slopes in different physical contexts.
overview.teacherInsight: Beware the "Graph as Picture" trap: students frequently mistake a graph's shape for the physical road or hill. Remind students that on a Speed vs. Time graph, a downward slope does not mean the skateboarder is going downhill—it means they are slowing down!

vocabulary.definition: A graph where vertical position represents physical altitude or height above ground.
A graph where vertical position represents instantaneous rate of motion.
The speed of an object in a given direction, corresponding to signed slope on a displacement graph.

practiceQuestions.question: On an Elevation vs. Time graph, what does a negative slope depict?
options: The object is physically descending in altitude
The object is traveling backwards in time
practiceQuestions.explanation: A negative slope means elevation is decreasing as time progresses, representing a descent.

practiceQuestions.question: On a Speed vs. Time graph, what does a horizontal segment above the axis represent?
options: Motion at a steady, constant speed
The object is stationary at rest
The object is accelerating at maximum power
The object is at elevation zero
practiceQuestions.explanation: On a speed graph, y represents speed. A horizontal segment means speed is constant over that time interval.

guidedExercises.title: Example 1: Graphing Elevation vs. Time for a Hiker
guidedExercises.problem: A hiker starts at a trailhead elevation of $500\text{ ft}$. She climbs at a steady rate of $300\text{ ft/hr}$ for 2 hours, takes a 1-hour lunch break at the scenic overlook, and then descends to elevation $200\text{ ft}$ over the next 2 hours. Formulate the piecewise function $E(t)$ and graph its coordinates.
guidedExercises.scaffolding: Find the elevation at the end of each interval to determine boundary coordinates $(t, E(t))$.

steps.label: Phase 1: Climb for $t \in [0, 2]$ hours
steps.explanation: Line segment connecting $(0, 500)$ to $(2, 1100)$ with slope $+300$.

steps.label: Phase 2: Lunch break for $t \in [2, 3]$ hours
steps.explanation: Horizontal line segment connecting $(2, 1100)$ to $(3, 1100)$ with slope $0$.

steps.label: Phase 3: Descent for $t \in [3, 5]$ hours to 200 ft
steps.explanation: Line segment connecting $(3, 1100)$ to $(5, 200)$ with slope $-450$.

guidedExercises.commonPitfall: Drawing a physical picture of the mountain or trail instead of graphing mathematical elevation against time. A curve going down and to the left is physically impossible because time never moves backward.

guidedExercises.title: Exercise 1: Water Level in Geometric Containers with Variable Diameters
guidedExercises.problem: Water is poured at a constant flow rate into an ink bottle shaped like a sphere with a narrow cylindrical neck at the top. Describe how the graph of height $h(t)$ vs. time $t$ behaves from empty to full.
guidedExercises.scaffolding: Where the container is wide, the water level rises slowly (flat slope). Where the container is narrow, the water level rises rapidly (steep slope).

steps.label: Bottom hemisphere (widening cross-section)
steps.explanation: Initially narrow at the very bottom (fast rise), then slows down as width expands to the equator.

steps.label: Top hemisphere (narrowing cross-section)
steps.explanation: As the sphere tapers toward the neck, height rises faster and faster.

steps.label: Cylindrical neck (constant cross-section)
steps.explanation: The narrow neck fills rapidly at a constant linear rate.

guidedExercises.finalAnswer: \text{The graph is S-shaped (inflection at sphere equator), terminating with a steep straight linear segment for the neck.}
guidedExercises.commonPitfall: Assuming constant volume inflow produces a constant height rise rate. Remember: $\text{Rate of height increase} = \frac{\text{Flow Rate}}{\text{Cross-Sectional Area}}$.
